analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $25 an hour and ends all subminimum wages.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2026 with four Democratic sponsors and referred to the Senate labor committee, the bill has had no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $12 for everyone on the effective date, then step up to $25 an hour over five years for large companies ($1 billion in revenue or 500+ employees) and over twelve years for smaller employers. After that, the minimum would automatically equal two-thirds of the national median hourly wage, so it rises with the economy. It would also phase out the separate lower wages allowed for tipped workers, newly hired teens, and workers with disabilities, eventually paying all of them the full minimum. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: Workers now earning at or near the $7.25 federal minimum, tipped workers whose federal cash wage is $2.13, newly hired workers under 20 who can legally be paid $4.25, and workers with disabilities paid under special certificates — millions of people who would see their wage floor climb in scheduled steps. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage, tipped, teen, and disabled workers

how_it_helps.text: The minimum wage rises to $12 for all covered workers on the effective date, then large employers must pay $15 after one year, $18 after two, $20 after three, $22.50 after four, and $25 after five.
Employers that are not large employers get a slower climb — $14, $16, $18, then $20 by year four — reaching $25 after twelve years.

After the phase-in, the minimum for both groups is set each year to the greater of the prior amount or two-thirds of the national median hourly wage calculated by the Labor Department from Bureau of Labor Statistics data, so it rises with the economy without another act of Congress.

Tipped workers' required cash wage climbs for large employers from $6 to the full minimum over five years, and for other employers rises $1.75 a year until it equals the full minimum; once parity is reached, the separate tipped minimum wage is repealed outright.
The bill writes into the law that employees keep their own tips and that employers must inform them of that right.

Workers with disabilities paid under special certificates start at $5 an hour and rise $1.75 a year to the full minimum; no new certificates may be issued, and the certificate system sunsets once wage parity is reached.
The $4.25 subminimum wage for newly hired workers under 20 is raised in the same stepwise fashion and repealed once it reaches the full minimum.
The Labor Department must publish notice of each scheduled increase at least 60 days in advance, giving employers and workers lead time.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost through higher payroll: large corporations first and fastest, restaurants and other tipped-wage businesses, sheltered-workshop operators, and small businesses more slowly. Some of the cost is likely to reach consumers through higher prices, and some employers may respond by cutting hours, positions, or automation. [S2]
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations, restaurants, and small employers

drawbacks.text: The schedule is steep by historical standards: the floor goes from $7.25 to $12 immediately and to $25 for large employers within five years, which is a much larger and faster jump than any previous federal increase.

Because a national $25 floor is the same in high-cost and low-cost regions, the relative shock falls hardest on employers and workers in low-wage local labor markets, where economists studying past large increases have found some job, hour, and automation losses alongside wage gains.
Restaurants lose the tipped-credit system entirely, not just at the phase-in point but as a matter of law, which is the largest structural cost increase in the bill for that industry.

The index to two-thirds of the national median wage raises the minimum automatically every year with no future vote, which supporters call protection against erosion and critics call removing the decision from Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are large and concrete: a scheduled, enforceable wage floor rising to $25 for millions of workers, and the end of every federal subminimum wage, including the $2.13 tipped wage and the disability certificate system. The costs are real but distributed: payroll increases for employers, likely price increases for consumers, and a risk — supported by research on past large increases but smaller than the wage gains in most studies — of job or hour losses for some marginal workers. The five-year timeline for large corporations and the twelve-year runway for small employers are designed to blunt that risk. On the whole, this is a deliberately structured, high-impact wage bill rather than a hastily designed one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in mid-July 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled. [S4]

narrative.text: Senator Christopher Murphy introduced the bill on July 14, 2026, joined by three other Democratic senators.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Four Democratic senators are listed as cosponsors, and no Republican has joined; Republicans hold 55 of 100 Senate seats.
The action history shows no further activity after the committee referral.
The Congress runs until January 3, 2027, so the bill technically remains alive, but no vote has been scheduled in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No final outcome has occurred yet, so no one has won or lost because of the bill itself. If it dies in committee at the end of this Congress — the most common fate for wage bills with no opposition-party support — employers paying near the current $7.25 minimum, restaurants using the $2.13 tipped wage, and holders of disability wage certificates would be the beneficiaries of inaction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, so far — no raise has happened.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Living Wage For All Act in the Senate on July 14, 2026.

for.name: 4 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Senate Republican did.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; with Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats and the bill parked in the Senate labor committee, no vote has been scheduled in either chamber.

industries.industry: Large corporations (retail, fast-food chains, warehouse and logistics employers)
industries.note: Any company with $1 billion in revenue or 500+ employees must go from a $7.25 floor to $25 an hour within five years — a direct, large payroll increase for the biggest low-wage employers, whose workers are the bill's main beneficiaries. [S2]

The bill phases out the tipped-credit system, under which the federal cash wage can be as low as $2.13, and eventually repeals the separate tipped minimum outright; servers and bartenders gain the full minimum. [S2]

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and employers holding disability wage certificates
industries.note: Section 14(c) certificates that let employers pay workers with disabilities below the minimum rise to $5 an hour immediately, climb to the full minimum, and are then abolished, ending a subminimum wage system those employers rely on. [S2]

Businesses under the $1 billion/500-employee threshold get a twelve-year runway to $25 instead of five, softening but not eliminating the cost increase; their lower-wage workers gain the same floor. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: With roughly five and a half months left in this Congress, no Republican cosponsor, and no committee action since the July referral, the bill is very unlikely to reach the Senate floor. Minimum wage bills without opposition-party support in a divided Senate have historically expired in committee. The realistic paths are expiration in January 2027, reintroduction in the next Congress, or its provisions being attached to a larger bill — none of which is currently signaled by the record.
